Pancreatic cancer precision treatments that save lives cost tens of thousands a month (https://www.theaustralian.com.au/health/medical/costs-of-pancreatic-cancer-drug-that-saved-dees-life-limit-access/news-story/999e5206e1ce5baf313b0bfeddf0e22b)
【turn1056news12】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 5 days ago; Dee Ozolins' journey from a terminal pancreatic cancer diagnosis to remission highlights the transformative potential and high cost of new precision cancer therapies. After a harrowing experience with surgery and chemotherapy, Dee learned her cancer had spread. However, genetic testing revealed a KRAS G12D mutation, making her eligible for a groundbreaking clinical trial using a KRAS inhibitor. The treatment stabilized her condition for over 18 months, offering hope where none existed. Yet, these drugs can cost up to $US40,000 a month and are not yet publicly subsidised in Australia, raising concerns about access and affordability. Pancreatic cancer, long underfunded and associated with poor survival rates, has recently seen promising breakthroughs. Experts like Michelle Stewart of Pancreatic Cancer Australia and Professor Andrew Wilson stress the necessity of timely access and systemic reforms to support equitable distribution of these life-extending treatments. Debates continue over how Australia's public health system can adapt to the rising costs of personalized medicine, amid growing pressure to bridge the gap between scientific innovation and healthcare accessibility. Dee’s story underscores the urgent need to update evaluation systems for new drugs to ensure that more lives can be saved.
Pancreatic cancer precision treatments that save lives cost tens of thousands a month
Date: Fri Oct 16 18:00:00 2026 UTC

Her weight had shrivelled to 35kg and she did not have the energy even to slice a carrot for the family dinner. Her cancer specialist gave her months to live. Little more than a year later she walked to the summit of Mt Kosciuszko and was able to enjoy games of pickleball with her friends. This incredible recovery from advanced pancreatic cancer was the result of treatment with a new class of drug - a drug that has implications for our whole health system. New treatments for cancers such as Dee's act with great precision, targeting specific genetic markers in the malignant tissues. These drugs, for the first time, offer enormous potential for thousands of Australians. However, they come at an enormous cost and prompt the question: Just how much is our health system prepared to pay to save a life? Dee, a young mother of two teenage girls, first noticed her symptoms just over two years ago when she was busy preparing for a major event at work. "I kept getting pain just under my rib cage, and I would have to sort of stretch out, and the pain wouldn't go away," she explained. "I kept thinking, once the project is over, I'll go and get it tested. I kept ignoring it until eventually I turned yellow." Suddenly worried, her husband took her to an emergency department where she was diagnosed with a blockage of the duct that drains bile from the liver. The blockage was cleared but, three months later, the pain returned and she was advised to have her gall bladder removed. It was during that second procedure that her specialist realised Dee's diagnosis was much more serious. Dee attended her specialist's offices after the operation. Assuming that she was about to be pronounced cured, her husband dropped her at the rooms on his way to the airport for an overseas surfing trip. "My mum was also away and my daughter, my oldest one, was doing the HSC so she was at home minding my youngest, and my poor sister was running around," Dee said. Alone and unsuspecting, Dee was given the news that she had an extremely serious cancer. Pancreatic cancer has a five-year survival rate of only 13 per cent. Shocked, she reached out to her sister, who had just emerged from the shower. "I rang my sister and just said, I've got cancer'," Dee recalls, "and I remember she was running out the door with wet hair. I rang her back and said 'no, you've got time to blow-dry it'. "I even said to the doctor, 'do I need to call my husband? Can I let him have his surf trip?'."So I had the highest doses possible of everything." The experience of the unremitting chemotherapy was shattering. Unable to eat, barely able to move, she lost all of her strength. "My poor children were just watching me when I was so ill for such a long time. I honestly believe my poor husband still has PTSD from it." Worse was to come. Dee and her family had expected that the combination of surgery and chemotherapy would rid her body of the cancer. That turned out to be a cruel misapprehension. A month after the treatment finally ended, Dee underwent a scan and prepared for a visit with her cancer specialist to discuss the results. "I'd bought him a gift and a card, thinking it was the end and we were getting good news," she remembers. Her husband was parking the car and, again, she went into the appointment alone. "I remember the oncologist saying the cancer had spread to my lungs." The revelation was shocking. "I actually asked him what the prognosis was and he said, 'without treatment, you have nine to 12 months. There's nothing else we can do unless we can find another treatment option'," she said. It was at this point that something incredible occurred. When the initial surgery had been done, six months before, the pancreatic cancer had been sent for genetic analysis. Dee had not even understood what the testing was for. "I didn't ask too much about it at the time," she said. "I thought it was just to make sure my children didn't have it. But my oncologist was fantastic, and he was always a few steps ahead, and thought I better be ready for Plan B." The testing had shown that Dee's pancreatic cancer cells had a genetic change - a mutation - known as KRAS G12D.Pancreatic cancer precision treatments that save lives cost tens of thousands a month
Date: Fri Oct 16 18:00:00 2026 UTC

 This meant the tumour might respond to an extraordinary new class of drugs that precisely curb the signals that drive cancer cells to multiply. Dee found that because her cancer carried this genetic change, she was potentially eligible to be treated as part of an experimental clinical trial of one of these new precision therapies. There were two places available on the trial for patients with advanced pancreatic cancer. "You've got to be ill, but not too ill," Dee explained. "So when I finally was accepted I actually didn't believe it. That was the first time I felt there was hope." Dee has been stabilised on the medication - which is a KRAS inhibitor that blocks the activity of proteins that promote tumour growth - for 18 months and counting. For as long as the clinical trial of her particular drug continues, the targeted medication is likely to keep working. But once the trial ends, she faces an uncertain outlook as to whether the vital medication, costing tens of thousands of dollars a month, will be publicly subsidised. The gap between public funding and the advent of innovative drugs is growing more acute for patients. Earlier this year the results of a precision new treatment for pancreatic cancers that carry the same mutation as Dee Ozolins' tumour were announced. A drug named Daraxonrasib , taken as a daily oral treatment, doubled the survival rate and extended the life for patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, a diagnosis previously considered untreatable. The announcement of these amazing results brought a standing ovation from an audience of seasoned cancer specialists. The downside? This treatment costs $US40,000 ($57,483) a month. I am a medical specialist and when I trained as a doctor, in the early 1980s, we were taught that pancreatic cancer was the most feared and untreatable cancer. Even our lectures were delivered in a tone of deep pessimism. Then the disease cut a swath through my own family. We have lost five members of my father's generation to pancreatic cancer, and as I talk with Dee about her own and her family's experience, everything she says resonates with me deeply. Since I come from a family at high risk of pancreatic cancer, I now closely follow advances in managing the deadly disease. For the first time in my almost 40-year career I have optimism for the future. My optimism is shared by Michelle Stewart, CEO of Pancreatic Cancer Australia - known as Pankind. "Pancreatic cancer is often diagnosed late, when it has already spread, and by that stage there are very limited treatment options," Michelle explained.Pancreatic cancer precision treatments that save lives cost tens of thousands a month
Date: Fri Oct 16 18:00:00 2026 UTC

 "Survival is not necessarily that long for somebody diagnosed with it so we don't have a lot of people talking about the disease. As a result it has kind of fallen in the too-hard basket for so many years." Because of this pervasive pessimism, investment in research into the disease has been pitifully low in Australia. "I think it's really upsetting that the investment in pancreatic cancer has been so low," Michelle said. "For so many years, we just weren't able to push forward. We couldn't get those breakthroughs." Fortunately, that now is changing and changing fast. "We're starting to see all the hard work that's been happening for many years actually turning into options and treatments for better patient outcomes," Michelle told me. "So it's really exciting that we're seeing all these new technologies coming through. "The challenge for us now is to make sure that people are able to access them in a timely manner. There's nothing worse than seeing this promise but not being able to get access to it." Steve Robson, Professor of obstetrics and gynaecology, has taken a blood test that could revolutionise the way one of Australia's most lethal cancers is managed. I asked Michelle, whose organisation, Pankind, aims to triple the survival from pancreatic cancer in Australian patients, how we can put a price on human life. "I think it's really difficult," she said. "Obviously, the costs of developing these treatments needs to be recouped. But to the person on the street who needs access to a medicine that's going to extend their life, there is no price that can be put on that." The economic implications of paying for these revolutionary life-extending treatments for cancer are potentially staggering and could weigh heavily on our already stretched health system. Professor Andrew Wilson is director of the University of Sydney's Centre for Health Policy and Economics and an expert in how we can afford new health technologies. I asked him how Australia can make these new cancer treatments affordable for the patients who most need them. "The problems are not unique to Australia," he said. "So we have to take an international perspective. "We've become much better at defining different types of cancer based on their genomic profile, and we can divide up cancers into smaller and smaller groups. So the number of patients we're treating with each particular type of therapy has gotten smaller, and the cost of those drugs are higher, in part because they're treating smaller numbers of patients. "The traditional thinking around cancer treatment was that you got your treatment and you were either cured or you weren't. That was basically it and your treatment was over.PBAC, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee , is the group that makes recommendations to the health minister on what medications Australia's flagship PBS should subsidise . While this plays out, thousands of Australians who face a diagnosis like Dee Ozolins and her family do, are making decisions about what treatments they want and how they can pay for them. "It feels like we're cheaper if we're dead," Dee said. Her words shocked me. Perhaps they shouldn't. "They need to look at beyond the actual cost of the medication," she continued. "The new drugs coming through are giving people like me quality of life again. We're working again. We're contributing members of society. We're living every single day. "The fact is that if I was not on a trial I would be bankrupt. I would have to go overseas for my treatment, which people do, so we need to update our systems and our processes to evaluate these new medications because the world has changed." Michelle Stewart, who in her role as CEO of Pankind sees patients around the country who are dealing with pancreatic cancer, also has strong feelings about how we fund these new treatments. "Australians are waiting for medicines that could save their lives, and the system for approving them is too slow, currently," she said. "It takes 22 months to get a new drug approved or reimbursed in Australia. With pancreatic cancer only 22 per cent of people will survive two years. The system is not set up to help the patients that we need to help today." Professor Steve Robson is a medical specialist, researcher and health economist. Cavernous Malformation - 20 Questions Answered (https://www.alliancetocure.org/home/for-patients/newly-diagnosed/20-questions-answered-cavernous-malformation-angioma-cavernoma/)
【turn1056search11】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; 7 days ago — Newly diagnosed with cavernous malformation? Get answers to 20 common questions about symptoms, treatment , and living with this condition.
This page will help you understand the condition and make informed choices about your care. You may want to share this page with family members or others who care about you so they can better understand the condition.

Jump to a topic:

  * Understanding CCM
  * Bleeding (hemorrhage)
  * Your care and treatment
  * Pregnancy & Children
  * Living with cavernous malformation

Patient stories: Ross · Vanessa · John · Joyce · Kathryn

### What is a cavernous malformation?

Cavernous malformations are made up of abnormal blood vessels. They are made of capillaries (the smallest blood vessels in the body). Blood moves through cavernous malformations very slowly. They look like raspberries and have very thin walls. Those thin walls can leak, and blood may enter nearby brain or spinal cord tissue. They are not cancerous but are sometimes called vascular tumors because they can grow.

#### Where they form

Most cavernous malformations occur in the cerebral lobes, the upper part of the brain. Cavernous malformations may also occur in the brainstem, the part of the brain that connects to the spinal cord. The spinal cord is the least common place for a cavernous malformation that causes symptoms. Cavernous malformations can cause severe symptoms and complications when they hemorrhage (bleed).

Image: A cavernous malformation removed during surgery. It looks like a small, dark red raspberry.

### What symptoms can a cavernous malformation cause?

Symptoms from cavernous malformations vary from person to person. Location plays a large role, since different parts of the brain and spinal cord control different functions. Size and behavior matter too — a small, stable cavernous malformation is less likely to cause symptoms than a larger one or one that is actively bleeding. Some cavernous malformations cause no symptoms at all.

If more than one cavernous malformation is found incidentally, it is a good idea to have regular follow-up visits with a doctor. This helps you maintain a relationship with a care provider in case you develop symptoms later.

Even though this can feel scary, it’s important to know that many stable lesions stay stable for years and never cause problems. Surgery is rarely used unless a lesion is causing symptoms, since surgery carries its own risks.

### What is a sporadic cavernous malformation?

Most cavernous malformations happen by chance and are not passed down in families. These are called sporadic cavernous malformations.

People with this type usually have:

  * Only one cavernous malformation
  * No family history of the condition

Family members, including children, of a person with sporadic cavernous malformation are not more likely to have cavernous malformations than anyone else.

#### How doctors check

To check for this condition, your doctor may order an MRI scan with a special type of image called susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI). This type of imaging can help doctors see smaller cavernous malformations. If no additional cavernous malformations are found on SWI, this is reassuring that the person likely has a sporadic cavernous malformation.

### What causes multiple cavernous malformations?

Some people have more than one cavernous malformation. This can happen for a few reasons:

  * The most common reason is familial cavernous malformation. People with this condition are born with a higher chance of developing multiple cavernous malformations over time. Familial cavernous malformation is caused by a mutation (change) in the CCM1 (also called KRIT1), CCM2, or CCM3 (also called PDCD10) genes.
  * Some people develop multiple cavernous malformations after radiation therapy for brain cancer.
Vanessa was two weeks into her second semester at fashion school in New York City when a brain bleed changed her life. An MRI traced the bleed to a cerebral cavernous malformation in her thalamus (a part of the brain that helps control movement and sensation), with two more nearby. All three lesions were clustered together around a developmental venous anomaly (DVA), which is not uncommon with cavernous malformations. Doctors often talk about bleeding risk in terms of yearly risk or five-year risk. Many cavernous malformations never cause a serious bleed. However, if a cavernous malformation has already bled once, the chance of another bleed is higher. The risk is greatest in the first five years after the first bleed, and then it slowly goes down over time and may return close to the level of cavernous malformations that have never bled. Very small cavernous malformations do not usually bleed.

Image: MRI showing a cavernous malformation in the brainstem

### Does anything increase my hemorrhage risk?

A bleed that causes new symptoms, also called a symptomatic hemorrhage, is the most serious problem that can happen with a cavernous malformation. About 1 in 4 people diagnosed with this condition will have at least one bleed.

#### Medicines and hormones

You may wonder if certain medications, like blood thinners, increase your risk. Current research shows that blood thinners do not seem to increase the risk of bleeding for most people. However, you should always talk with your healthcare provider before starting or stopping any medication.

For the most up-to-date information, visit the hemorrhage section of the Alliance to Cure Cavernous Malformation website. If you have questions about your own risk, talk with your healthcare provider. They can help you understand what is best for your situation.

Image: John

### Patient Story: John

Living with a Spinal Cavernous Malformation

John had already lived with a cavernous malformation diagnosis for four years when he boarded a flight home from a family trip. His brainstem CCM had bled once, leaving him with symptoms that improved over months but never fully resolved. He had learned to live with them.

Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22062)
【turn1056academia14】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline
Authors: Daniel Palacios, Guantong Qi, Mikael Guzman Karlsson, Shawntel K. David, Mohammed Sameeruddin, Bernhard Suter, Zhandong Liu, Davut Pehlivan, Hu Chen
Date: Thu Oct 15 15:24:47 2026

Objective: Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. We developed a dual large language model (LLM) consensus pipeline to extract 18 treatment-response phenotypes, comprising 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features, and medication refusal, from clinical notes. Materials and Methods: We analyzed 26,763 notes from 108 patients with confirmed sustained trofinetide exposure at Texas Children's Hospital. The pipeline filters notes by keyword, classifies each through two LLMs requiring consensus, and aggregates a patient-by-timepoint matrix. Architecture and prompt were selected on a diarrhea development set, then frozen and applied to the other 17 phenotypes with the phenotype definition substituted, as an out-of-sample test. The reported prompt comparison scores 183 expert-labeled cells. Results: A prompt requiring diarrhea to be active and severe performed best (84.2 $\pm$ 0.0% accuracy; F1 = 0.674), 47 percentage points above regular-expression matching ($p < 0.0001$). Expert reviewers judged six of the pipeline's calls per phenotype, three positive and three negative, and agreed with 90.2% (92/102). The 13 Rett clinical features are manifestations of the disorder itself rather than adverse effects of trofinetide. Gross and fine motor impairment, language/communication, and stereotypy were documented present in 92-100% of patients at every visit. Discussion: In-context LLM extraction captured multi-domain treatment responses. The outcome is documented presence at each visit, not a direction-of-change judgment. Conclusion: Coupling in-context LLM reasoning with a consensus architecture offers a scalable alternative to keyword and regular-expression extraction for real-world evidence, adapting to new phenotypes and medications through configuration alone.

Title: Trial design considerations in the face of overdispersion and time-varying event rates: a meta-regression approach with an application in asthma
Authors: Bohua Chen, Christian Röver, Stefan Andreas, Christian Taube, Tim Friede
Date: Thu Oct 15 07:44:40 2026

**Purpose:** Relative changes in event rates are a common primary endpoint in confirmatory asthma trials. Reliable assumptions about baseline event rates and extra-Poisson variability are essential for sample size planning. We synthesize placebo-group exacerbation data, evaluate calendar-time trends, and assess implications for trial design. **Methods:** We systematically reviewed randomized controlled trials reporting recurrent asthma exacerbations and extracted control-group outcomes classified by placebo type or asthma severity. Hierarchical negative binomial models accommodated heterogeneous reporting formats and jointly modeled event rates and overdispersion. We compared separate subgroup models with covariate-based models and used meta-regression to adjust for calendar-time trends. Trial design implications were illustrated using the NAVIGATOR trial. **Results:** Sixty-two trials met the inclusion criteria. The estimated relative change in annualized exacerbation rates was -1.8% per year (95% CrI: -7.5%, 4.3%), corresponding to a 16.5% decrease per decade (95% CrI: -54.2%, 52.2%). Substantial between-study heterogeneity in event rates and overdispersion was observed. Within-trial overdispersion was estimated as 1.53 (95% CrI: 0.60, 2.83). In an illustrative phase III design scenario, sample size requirements were sensitive to the target subgroup and uncertainty in the predicted event rate and overdispersion. **Conclusion:** Event rates in clinical trials exhibit considerable heterogeneity and potential temporal variation, and overdispersion is a critical design parameter. Comprehensive modelling of recurrent-event endpoints allows for evidence-based and robust sample size calculations and trial design.

Title: SurvICL: a Foundation Model for in-context Survival Analysis
Authors: Julie Alberge, Linus Bleistein, Judith Abécassis, Marine Le Morvan, Gaël Varoquaux, David Holzmüller
Date: Thu Oct 15 17:16:56 2026

Tabular foundation models (TFMs) now outperform gradient-boosted trees in classification and regression. Yet in survival analysis, which predicts when an event occurs from censored data, often on small clinical cohorts, we find that no existing TFM beats the half-century-old Cox model. We address this issue by introducing SurvICL, a TFM that predicts survival curves in-context. SurvICL is pretrained on purely synthetic datasets generated from a novel flexible proportional-odds prior that outperforms other prior types in our ablation study. Unlike most other survival models, SurvICL is trained with a plain quantile regression loss, which is possible because its synthetic pre-training data generator can provide uncensored event times. Additionally, we introduce the largest survival benchmark to date spanning 103 datasets. On the 63 datasets held out from all design decisions, SurvICL outperforms 20 tree-based, deep, and foundation-model baselines without any tuning: it wins 82.9\% of pairwise comparisons in integrated Brier score, against 71.3\% for the runner-up, the Cox model, and is the first model to rank above Cox on small datasets.
